title: Estimands and Inference in Cluster-Randomized Vaccine Trials
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how causal effects should be defined and estimated in cluster-randomized vaccine trials when whole clusters are randomized but individuals within clusters may choose whether to participate. The core question is methodological: which vaccine effects are actually identifiable and interpretable under this design, especially when interference or spillover is possible within clusters. The authors argue that careful specification of estimands is necessary so trial goals, analysis, and interpretation align.

The paper develops a theoretical framework for estimating overall, indirect, and total effects in cluster-randomized trials with self-selection into vaccination, under assumptions such as no interference between clusters and participation behavior being unaffected by cluster assignment because of blinding. It also shows that a naive comparison between vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals within treated clusters does not identify a causal direct effect in general, because self-selection can induce confounding. The paper therefore distinguishes estimable effects from non-identifiable ones.

As an illustration, the authors use a cluster-randomized typhoid vaccine trial in Kolkata, India, conducted from 2004 to 2006, in which 80 clusters were randomized to typhoid vaccine or hepatitis A control vaccine. Because individual-level data were unavailable, they simulated a dataset to match published cluster-level summary statistics. They report risk-difference estimates over two years: an overall effect of -2.49 typhoid cases per 1000 people, an indirect effect of -1.29 per 1000 non-participants, and a total effect of -3.30 per 1000 participants. A naive direct-effect estimate was positive, but the authors explicitly state this should not be interpreted causally because participant versus non-participant comparisons are confounded.

For the user's verification purpose, this is not a ChatGPT, writing, motivation, or high-school study, and it is not the alleged 2026 education RCT. It contains no students, no writing outcomes, no motivation measures, and no 25-plus-25 secondary-school experiment. It should therefore be excluded from any quantitative synthesis on ChatGPT-based writing feedback in high school as an irrelevant, non-education methodological vaccine-trial paper.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a biostatistics/methods paper on estimands and inference in cluster-randomized vaccine trials, not an education or ChatGPT intervention study. It contains no high-school writing experiment, no motivation outcomes, and no relevant educational sample; for the user's verification purpose, it is a clear retrieval mismatch and cannot contribute evidence to a synthesis on ChatGPT-based writing feedback.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no educational intervention impact and no student writing or motivation outcomes. Therefore it provides no usable impact estimate for the target review question and should not be included in any quantitative synthesis of ChatGPT-based writing feedback in high school.
